clue.text: Firearm produced by companion in Derbyshire town

indicators.note: the companion is placed in the middle of the town's name

parts.note: Matlock is a spa town in Derbyshire
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A gun turned out by somebody's friend in a Peak District town.
explanation.walkthrough: Matlock is a spa town in Derbyshire, an English county; CH, Companion of Honour, is a British honour that crossword setters use for 'companion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A matchlock is an early type of musket fired by a slow-burning match.

clue.text: Compete with army medic to obtain picture

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, an army doctor
to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: An army doctor competes to obtain a painting.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture is a film, as in going to the pictures, which a movie is.

clue.text: Harass bishops, say, in breach of duty

indicators.note: in places the chess pieces inside the legal wrong

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong, a breach of a duty in law
bishops are chessmen, so they are examples of men

explanation.surface: Clergy harassed in a case of negligence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bishops, say' points to chess: bishops are examples of men, the chess pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To torment someone is to harass or plague them persistently.

clue.text: Judge hirsute growth — it gives rise to anguish

parts.note: to hear a case is to judge it
tache is British slang for a moustache, a hairy growth

explanation.surface: A judge's moustache causes him great pain.
explanation.walkthrough: TACHE is informal British for moustache; 'it gives rise to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartache is emotional anguish or grief.

clue.text: Old thin doctor's strange description of some dentistry

indicators.note: strange signals the letters are put into an odd new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A gaunt elderly doctor's odd account of dental work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges O, THIN and DOCTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Orthodontic describes the branch of dentistry that corrects crooked teeth and jaws.

clue.text: Hide and take forty winks

definitions.meaning: the hide or skin of a young animal

explanation.definitionFit: Kip is a trade term for the skin of a calf and British slang for sleeping.

clue.text: Thrash son in fit of temper

indicators.note: the son is set within the fit of temper

parts.note: bate is an old word for a rage or bad temper

explanation.surface: A father beats his boy during an outburst of anger.
explanation.walkthrough: BATE, a dated British word for a temper, takes S inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To baste someone is to beat or thrash them soundly, a sense separate from cooking.

clue.text: Was his Don Juan the work of another man?

definitions.text: Was his Don Juan the work of another man?

parts.words: Was his Don Juan the work of another man?
parts.note: the poem's author's name splits into a word for authorship and a short man's name, so the question wonders whether someone else wrote it

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a famous poem was really written by its supposed author.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Juan is a long comic poem; the poet's surname read as two words says it was written by a fellow called Ron.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron, the Romantic poet, wrote the satirical epic Don Juan.

clue.text: From house, managed to get up for class

parts.note: a semi is a semi-detached house

indicators.note: in a down clue, get up means the word rises, read from bottom to top

parts.note: ran means managed

explanation.surface: A student goes from home to a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: A SEMI is a British semi-detached house; 'to get up' turns RAN into NAR in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminar is a class where a small group meets to discuss a subject.

clue.text: Aim to get boy, knowing it's forever

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal
Les is a boy's name, short for Leslie
sly means knowing or cunning

explanation.surface: A parent aims to have a son, knowing that it is permanent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' and 'it's' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Endlessly means without end, continuing for all time.

clue.text: Unsophisticated priest rejected poet not writing English

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the priest's title is read backwards

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, a priest's title

indicators.note: not writing English means the letter for English is left out of the poet's name

parts.note: Dante, the Italian poet

explanation.surface: A naive cleric turns away a poet who refuses to write in English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns REV into VER; 'not writing English' drops E from DANTE, leaving DANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdant literally means green, and green is used for someone raw and inexperienced.

clue.text: Egyptian monument originally painted by two retired women

indicators.note: originally signals taking just the opening letter of the next word
retired means withdrawn or gone back, so each woman's name is read backwards

parts.note: Mary, a common woman's name
Di, short for Diana, another woman's name

explanation.surface: An ancient tomb first decorated by a pair of elderly ladies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns each woman's name round where it stands rather than reversing the whole run, and 'by two' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The pyramids of Giza are the most famous ancient monuments of Egypt.

clue.text: Item in sports programme, one in seventeen

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the letters of the next word

explanation.surface: One of seventeen fixtures listed on the sports day schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is found in the letters of 'seventeen', between the first S and the final EN.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is a single contest or race listed in an athletics or sports meeting.

clue.text: Command soldiers take in during social event

parts.note: OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers

indicators.note: during means the small word comes within the social event

parts.note: a dance is a social gathering
taken as written

explanation.surface: An order for troops to drop in at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' is only a link joining the soldiers to the rest; OR, other ranks, is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative decree or order, especially a local regulation.

clue.text: Dirty Scouse's terrible rudeness

indicators.note: terrible signals the letters are mangled into another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A grubby Liverpudlian's awful bad manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges DIRTY and SCOUSE; a Scouse is a person from Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Discourtesy is impolite or rude behaviour.

clue.text: Paddy's blue-eyed boy?

definitions.meaning: a paddy is a fit of temper, also called a ... in older British usage
a blue-eyed boy is a favourite, someone's darling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like a name for an Irishman, but in British slang a paddy is a tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a pet is a sulk or huff, and a pet is a favoured person.

clue.text: Piglike mammals turn up fungus, getting tooth decay

indicators.note: in a down clue, turn up means the word reads upwards

parts.note: a cep is an edible mushroom, the porcini
caries is the medical word for tooth decay

explanation.surface: Wild pigs root out mushrooms and get rotten teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn up' turns CEP into PEC.
explanation.definitionFit: Peccaries are hoofed mammals of the Americas that look like pigs.

clue.text: Puzzles about saint engendering fight

indicators.note: about means the puzzles go around the saint

parts.note: crosswords are word puzzles

explanation.surface: Arguments over which saint the puzzle-setters should honour lead to a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: S goes in the middle of CROSSWORDS, between CROSS and WORDS; 'engendering' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To cross swords means to argue or come into conflict with someone, from duelling.

clue.text: City church seized by one inflicting defeat?

indicators.note: seized by means the church is held within the other word

parts.note: to worst is to defeat, so a worster defeats
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church captured by a conquering army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one inflicting defeat' is a made-up agent noun from the verb worst, to beat; Worcester is in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Worcester is a cathedral city in the west of England.

clue.text: Sure thing in African state, queen being music-lover

indicators.note: in places the sure thing inside the African country

parts.note: Congo is a country in central Africa
cert, short for certainty, is British slang for a sure thing
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual abbreviation for the Queen

explanation.surface: A dead cert in an African country, with the queen fond of music.
explanation.walkthrough: CERT is British slang for a certainty, as in a horse that is a dead cert.
explanation.definitionFit: A concertgoer attends concerts regularly, so is someone who loves music.

clue.text: Figure of horse exhibited in middle of day

indicators.note: exhibited in means the horse appears within midday

parts.note: noon is the middle of the day
a nag is a horse

explanation.surface: A horse is shown at a fair at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' is a geometric shape here, not a number or a person's outline.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonagon is a geometrical figure with nine sides.

clue.text: Authority, for example

definitions.meaning: having a ... is having power or influence in a decision
... introduces an example, as in 'take, ..., London'

explanation.definitionFit: Say means both a right to influence a matter and, informally, for instance.

clue.text: RA rules developed like some of Dali's paintings

indicators.note: developed suggests the letters have been worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Royal Academy rules evolved to suit Dali's style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developed' rearranges RA and RULES.
explanation.definitionFit: Dali was a leading Surrealist, so many of his paintings are dreamlike and bizarre.

clue.text: One may broadcast girl's light-weight introduction to radio

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
an ounce is a small unit of weight

indicators.note: introduction to means just the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A young woman gives a short opening talk on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on 'girl's' adds no letter; R comes from 'introduction to radio'.
explanation.definitionFit: An announcer is a person who presents or reads items on radio or television.

clue.text: They employ heartless doorkeepers

indicators.note: heartless means a letter from the middle of the word is taken out

parts.note: ushers keep doors and show people to their seats

explanation.surface: Employers callously treating their porters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes H, from the middle, out of USHERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Users are those who use something, and to use is to employ.

clue.text: Return unaccompanied across river to join up

indicators.note: across means the turned word spans the river letter, holding it within
Return means the word for unaccompanied is read backwards

parts.note: lone means alone, unaccompanied

explanation.surface: Coming back alone over the water in order to enlist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' turns LONE into ENOL, and R goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up or register as a member, as joining up is.

clue.text: Knowing about set-up in pastureland

indicators.note: in means the turned word sits within the pasture

parts.note: a ley is land temporarily under grass for grazing

indicators.note: in a down clue, set-up means the word is raised and read upwards

parts.note: re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Wise to a scheme on the farm.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'set-up' raises the short word so it reads upwards; a ley is a British farming term for temporary grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: Leery means wary or suspicious, someone knowing who is not easily fooled.

clue.text: French painter's right of entry

annotationWithheld.why: French painter's right of entry: INGRES + S, where 'painter's' both names the painter and supplies the S of the possessive, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Child's problem not everybody mentioned

indicators.note: mentioned signals the word is as spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: some means not all people

explanation.surface: A child's difficulty that not everyone talks about.
explanation.walkthrough: SOME and SUM are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum is an arithmetic problem set for a schoolchild.

clue.text: Army engineers leave first, one going over the top

indicators.note: first says the leave part comes before the engineers
going means the one is departing from the word for leave

parts.note: to exit is to leave
I is the Roman numeral one
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: Sappers depart first, one of them going over the top of the trench.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps. 'Army engineers' tempts you to RE; the full corps name is needed, and 'first' orders the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the top is an idiom for excessive or exaggerated, which is what extreme means.

clue.text: Hollow space? Not out in South America

indicators.note: in means the batting term sits between South and America

parts.note: US is the United States, America
a batsman not out is still in

explanation.surface: A cricketer not dismissed in South America finds an empty hole.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who is not out is still in, so 'Not out' supplies the inserted word.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinus is a cavity, especially one of the air-filled spaces in the skull bones.

clue.text: Like some whisky a man knocked back inside Henchard's office

indicators.note: inside means the a-and-man piece goes within the whisky word

parts.note: malt whisky tastes malty

indicators.note: knocked back means the man's name is turned round

parts.note: Roy is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man downs some malty whisky in the office of a Hardy character.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Henchard is the title character of Thomas Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge, so his office is that of mayor; only the man's name is turned, not the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Henchard held the post of mayor in Hardy's novel, and a mayoralty is that office.
